getting_started.title: Getting started
getting_started.content:
Slate

Slate is the studio's pipeline and its people system in one window. Your studio may start it as the full suite, or as the VFX app or the Operations app, which show fewer screens. The help lists the screens of the app you opened.

GroupScreens
Production (VFX app) Build & Ingest, CAP Rename, Stock Viewer, Timeline Viewer, VFX Dashboard, Scheduling, Bidding
People and IT (Operations app) Attendance, Leave, Joining & Leaving, Hardware, Licences, IT Support, Deployment, Users & Roles, Admin Panel
In both Home, Settings, Tester Panel and Workspace Info (where your role has them)

What you see depends on who you are

There is no mode switch and no permission warning. A screen your role does not use is absent rather than greyed out, and some entries open a different screen for different people:

EntryMost people getHR or IT get
LeaveTheir balance and a request buttonThe approval queue as well, plus the calendar and the year end
IT SupportTheir own tickets and repliesThe service desk
Joining & LeavingNo entry at allTheir team's half of the checklist

So if somebody describes a button you cannot find, you are probably both right. A change to your role shows the next time you sign in.

Keyboard

KeysDoes
Ctrl+K or Ctrl+PSearch or jump: screens, actions and shots
Ctrl+1 … Ctrl+9Go to a sidebar row by its position (group headings count as rows)
F5 or Ctrl+RRefresh the screen you are on
Ctrl+Shift+SSettings
Ctrl+Shift+DDiagnostics: which database and shared folder this machine reached
F1Help for the screen you are on
F11Full screen
EscClose a dialog or this window

The sidebar folds to icons with the arrow at its foot, and a category heading folds its group away when you click it. Tables sort when you click a column heading, and most have a search box above them.

The header

The bell beside Help collects your notifications — shots assigned to you, new scans, replies to your requests. The number on it is what you have not read yet.

The dot and figure show the round trip to the studio database in milliseconds — single digits is a healthy network, three digits means something is congested.

Sync appears only when Slate is working offline on this machine's local copy (LOCAL MODE). It sends the changes you made offline to the studio database and brings everybody else's back. With the studio database connected every change is shared the moment it is saved, so there is nothing to sync and the button is not shown.

Leaving and signing out

If a screen has unsaved changes, or an ingest or rename is still running, Slate asks before it closes or signs you out. Signing out or closing Slate does not punch you out of Attendance.

When something is wrong

"Can't reach the studio database". A screen could not read from the database. Your work is safe; the screen fills in when the connection is back, and Try again asks straight away.

"LOCAL MODE". Slate could not reach the studio database when it started and is working on a local copy. You can keep working and nothing is lost, but nobody else sees it until you Sync. Tell IT.

"Could not open …" or "Could not load …". Something went wrong on that screen. Press Try again; if it keeps happening, press Copy details for IT and paste them into a ticket.

Anything else. Raise it in IT Support rather than messaging somebody — a ticket carries a clock; a message does not. Include the version from Workspace Info, the first thing IT will ask.

home.title: Home
home.content:
Home

The opening screen. It gathers what you are most likely to want first, from the screens you have — nothing on it opens anything your role cannot reach.

Quick launch

Tiles for your most-used screens. Only screens that are in your sidebar appear.

My recent tasks

Shots assigned to you on the dashboard, in any department. Click one to open it on the VFX Dashboard. "No shots assigned to you" means exactly that — it is not an error. If you believe you have work, the dashboard's Scope: My Shots shows the same list; assignment is by person, so ask the coordinator to check the shot is assigned to your account.

Live studio figures

Read from the studio database, so they are the same figures your supervisor sees:

FigureCounts
Active projectsProjects not marked finished or archived
Pending reviewShots sitting in a review status
People in todayPeople who have punched in today and not out
Open IT ticketsTickets not yet resolved, studio-wide
Upcoming leaveApproved leave starting in the next two weeks

In the Operations app Home also carries your punch in and out.

Every figure reading zero when you expect otherwise usually means LOCAL MODE rather than a quiet studio — a local copy has no studio in it. The header says when Slate is working offline.

workspace_info.title: Workspace Info
workspace_info.content:
Workspace Info

What this particular copy of Slate is running: the version, where it is installed, which database it actually reached, and which plugins loaded.

Why you would open it

To answer "which version are you on?" — the first question IT ask on any ticket, and the one nobody can ever answer. It is on this screen. Copying it into the ticket saves a round trip and often the whole investigation, because half of all reported faults are a machine that never took an update.

To check the plugin system. This tab is itself a plugin, shipped as a working example. If it is in your sidebar, the plugin machinery is healthy.

Reading it

The card lists the runtime context Slate handed the plugin: the signed-in user, the workspace root, and the active database mode.

Database mode is the line worth a glance. If it says SQLite and your studio runs PostgreSQL, this machine is on its local fallback copy. Everything will appear to work and none of it is reaching anybody else. That is worth a ticket on its own.

folder_creator.title: Build & Ingest
folder_creator.content:
Build & Ingest

Turn a client drive into a project, and keep feeding it as more arrives.

Building a new project

  1. Project Code / Name — PRJ_001, or whatever the studio uses. This becomes the top folder.
  2. Source — the client or incoming drive.
  3. Reel — leave it empty and Slate works it out from the folder names on the drive, or type one (REEL_01) to force it.
  4. Template — decides the folder structure every shot gets. Templates are chosen and managed on this screen.
  5. Press the build button.

Copy or move

Copy is the default: files are copied into the project and checked, and the client drive is left exactly as it was, so a failed ingest costs time and not data. Move is an option for when the source is a scratch copy you no longer need; the check before it starts says which one will happen.

The second delivery, and the third

Use Update & Ingest New Files from then on. Each delivery is brought in as a new scan version next to what is already there, so earlier plates are never overwritten and you can always see which delivery a frame came from.

While it is running

Pause, Resume and Stop act between frames, so a paused or stopped ingest never leaves a half-written plate.

You can leave the tab and do something else; the job carries on and the progress is there when you come back. If you close Slate or sign out while it is running, Slate asks first and, if you go ahead, stops it at the next safe point.

Image sequences

A 1,200-frame EXR sequence is one item to Slate, not 1,200 files. That is why the counts are smaller than the file count on the drive. A single still image is a still, not a sequence.

If something does not land

Files Slate cannot classify are listed in the report at the end of the ingest rather than dropped — unrecognised and ignored files are named there so you can place them by hand.

rename_tool.title: CAP Rename
rename_tool.content:
CAP Rename

Batch renaming, in two modes. Both build a full preview first, and the preview is the point: read it before you press the button.

Search and replace

Find a string anywhere in the filenames and replace it.

  • Find — shot_v01
  • Replace with — shot_v02
  • Case sensitive — when ticked, Shot will not match shot

The preview shows the old name and the new name side by side for every file it will touch. It is a preview, not an editor: to change a name, change the settings above it. If two files would end up with the same name, or a name is not allowed (slashes, ..), Slate says so and refuses the whole operation rather than overwriting one file with another.

Serialize (make sequence)

Renumber a set of files into a clean, padded sequence.

  • Base name — shot_010_v01_
  • Padding — the target number of digits. 4 gives 0001.
  • Start — the first frame number.

Useful when a vendor delivers frames numbered from something arbitrary, or with inconsistent padding that breaks every tool downstream.

One row per file

Every file is its own row in the preview, so you see exactly what each frame will be called.

Undo

Every rename writes an undo script, undo_rename_<date>_<time>.bat, next to the files, line by line as it goes. Run it to put the old names back; it covers the files renamed so far even if the rename stopped half way. Renaming happens on disk, so still read the preview; if you are unsure, try it on a copy of a handful of files first.

If you close Slate while a rename is running, Slate waits for it to finish rather than leave files half renamed.

stock_browser.title: Stock Viewer
stock_browser.content:
Stock Viewer

The studio's stock library: footage, elements, textures — anything reused across jobs. Three panels: filters on the left, the gallery in the middle, the inspector on the right.

Finding something

Search reaches into the metadata as well as the filename, so 4K or smoke finds clips nobody thought to name that way.

Asset Filters in the sidebar narrow by type. Favorites keeps the handful you come back to. The library is paged, so a very large one loads as you scroll rather than making you wait for all of it.

The inspector

Select a clip and the right panel shows a preview and the facts you actually need before using it:

  • Resolution
  • FPS
  • Duration
  • Tags

These are read from the file itself, not typed in, so they are right even when the filename lies. Analyzing... means Slate is still reading it; the figures appear when it finishes.

Tags

Tags are how a library stays usable once it is large. They are shared with the studio rather than local to you, so tagging something well saves everybody else the search. Add them as you go — nobody ever comes back and tags a library later.

Adding to the library

Ingest brings a folder in. Fast Mode skips deep metadata analysis and is much quicker on a big drop — the clips are usable immediately and the detail fills in later. Pause works mid-ingest.

Refresh Library re-reads what is on disk, for when somebody has added files outside Slate.

Import and Export move a library definition between machines. Clear Library empties it entirely — it asks first, and it means the whole library, not the current filter.

Thumbnails

Generated in the background the first time an item is seen, then cached. A fresh library is slow to look at once and quick every time after.

A thumbnail that never appears usually means a format FFmpeg on this machine cannot read. Everything else about the item still works, and it is worth a ticket so IT can check the FFmpeg build.

shot_review.title: Timeline Viewer
shot_review.content:
Timeline Viewer

The reel laid out in order: plates reel by reel, with each department's render on its own layer directly beneath the plate it came from.

The shots come from the dashboard, so the timeline is always built from what production is actually tracking — not from whatever happens to be sitting in a folder.

Building a lineup

Pick the project and the reel. Slate finds the current version of each shot and lays them out in shot order.

Playing it

Heavy EXR and DPX sequences are transcoded to a proxy in the background the first time, then scrub smoothly. The first play of a new shot waits for that once; every later play does not.

Cutting

Launch Editor opens the lineup in Olive, embedded inside the Slate window. If Olive is not installed the button is absent and Slate falls back to its own player — ask IT to run setup.bat, which fetches it.

Reviewing

Review happens in OpenRV, which is what the studio actually reviews in. The dashboard opens a shot there directly with its Review in RV button, and a verdict recorded in RV comes back into Slate against that shot.

There used to be a Shot Checker built into this tab. It is gone, on purpose — a second-rate viewer beside a real one only splits where notes end up.

dashboard.title: VFX Dashboard
dashboard.content:
VFX Dashboard

Every shot in the project, its status, and who has it. This is the screen production runs the job from.

Reading it

The counters along the top count the shots on screen by status, in workflow order: YTS, READY, WIP, SENT FOR REVIEW, RETAKE, APPROVED, OMIT, and No status. Click one to show only those shots; click it again to show them all. Counters that do not fit are under +N more.

Each department has its own column (Matte Painting, CG, Roto, Prep / Paint, Matchmove, Comp and the rest). A cell holds that department's status on that shot. Reel and Shot Name stay at the left when you scroll sideways. Hover a cell for the full text; a red target is overdue, amber is due within a week.

Narrowing it

ControlDoes
ScopeAll shots, My shots (if you are given work), your own department, or any other department
Search (Ctrl+F)Looks in every column: shot, reel, status, artists, scope of work, type, target, version, priority and the description
StatusOne status across the project, including No status
Column funnelHover a heading and click its funnel (or right-click the heading) to tick the values to show
GroupGroup by reel, status, artist or priority; click a group's heading to fold it
FiltersRules such as Client feedback contains warmer, all or any of them
List | BoardThe same shots as a table or as cards, one column per status

Whenever anything narrows the grid, N filters on · Clear says so. No shots match means the filters excluded everything, not that the project is empty; the button under it clears them. Switching project starts with no filters.

Changing something

Every change — typing in a cell, dropping a card on the board, a batch edit from the right-click menu, or Apply in the shot panel — waits as a pending edit. Changed rows are tinted and changed cells marked, and the button at the top right counts them: Save 3 changes (Ctrl+S). Ctrl+Z takes back the last change; taking back everything leaves nothing to save. Refresh keeps your pending edits.

If somebody else saved one of the same shots first, Slate stops and shows both sides. Keep theirs, re-apply mine loads their save and puts your other edits back on top for you to check and save. People allowed to force a save also get Overwrite with mine, which writes over theirs for those shots only.

Artists change one thing: the status of a department they are assigned to (their cells are tinted). That is saved at once, with an Undo on the message. Leads change their own department's columns.

Closing Slate, signing out or switching project with pending edits asks first, and offers to save them. When a shot becomes APPROVED, Slate offers to copy its comp renders to the shot's output folder.

Projects

Manage project holds what you are allowed to do: add or edit a project, set its root folder, create a blank sheet template, export to Excel. Admins and developers can Archive a project (hidden, its shots and history kept, and brought back from Show archived projects) or Delete permanently, which asks for the project code. The dashboard opens on the project you had open last.

Where the data lives

The studio database. Other people's changes arrive without a refresh; a shot you have pending edits on is never replaced, only marked with ⚠. The Excel sheet is a backup copy Slate writes to after each save — Backup saved 19:21 at the top says when, Backup failing that the sheet is locked or the share unreachable. Slate never reads the sheet back.

When the studio database cannot be reached, a red banner says so and the dashboard is read-only until it is back.

scheduling.title: Scheduling
scheduling.content:
Scheduling

The studio's milestones — turnovers, first passes, reviews, deliveries — who owns them, what waits on what, and how they sit on the calendar.

Three views of the same plan

ViewShows
TableEvery milestone with its project, dependency, dates, status, owner and department. Click a heading to sort.
TimelineA Gantt chart: one bar per milestone, grouped by project (click a project to fold it). Arrows run from what a milestone waits on to the milestone; a red arrow means it starts before that has ended. Overdue bars have a red outline, finished ones are faded. Weekly offs are shaded, studio holidays shaded amber (hover for the name), and a line marks today. Zoom by Day, Week or Month, with Ctrl + mouse wheel, or Fit; Export PNG… saves the picture.
PeopleOne lane per person: the milestones they own and their assignments from the VFX Dashboard, with their approved leave shaded as away. The list beside it names every problem: work planned while somebody is away, and days booked with more than a day of work.

The search box, the Project, Status and Owner filters and Show archived projects apply to all three views, and the selection follows you between them.

Adding and changing milestones

Add milestone asks for the project, a name (up to 120 characters, unique within the project), what it depends on, its dates and status, and optionally an owner, a department and the effort in artist days. The form checks as you type and keeps Save switched off, saying why, until the milestone makes sense: the end cannot be before the start, and nothing can start before what it waits on has ended. A date on a weekend or a holiday is pointed out. A milestone can only wait on milestones of its own project.

Double-click a milestone (or select it and press Edit…) to change it. Delete… asks first; anything that waited on a deleted milestone is kept and simply no longer depends on it.

Change status… works on every selected milestone and offers Undo for a few seconds afterwards. Marking something Completed while what it waits on is still open asks first. The statuses are Scheduled, In Progress, On Hold, Blocked, Completed and Cancelled.

Shifting dates

Shift dates… moves the selected milestone and shows, before anything is saved, every milestone that moves with it, the ones that stay and why, and any dependency the move would break. You choose:

  • Working days (weekly offs and holidays are stepped over) or calendar days;
  • whether what follows is pushed only as far as it has to (any slack is kept) or moved by the same amount;
  • whether completed and cancelled milestones move too (normally they stay where they are).

Breaking a dependency needs an explicit tick. Everything is saved together — all of it or none of it — and Undo puts the old dates back. Dragging a bar on the Timeline, or its right-hand edge, opens the same preview.

Owners, leave and the dashboard

The People view reads the dashboard's assignments (artist, department, bid days and target date) to draw who is on what; change those on the VFX Dashboard. Only approved leave is shown as away — pending leave has not been decided, so chase the approver rather than planning around a request that may be refused. Giving a milestone an owner who has approved leave in its dates is allowed, but the form says so: it should be a decision, not a surprise.

Who can change the plan

Anybody whose role opens Scheduling can see it. Adding, editing, deleting, changing status and shifting need the Edit the schedule ability on the role; without it the tab says Read-only and the bars cannot be dragged. Every change is written to the history with who made it.

bidding.title: Bidding
bidding.content:
Bidding

What each job is priced at before it is agreed, every revision of that price, and — once it is won — how the work on the dashboard is tracking against it.

Building a bid

New bid opens the bid editor. Choose the project and the client, then build the bid out of lines: a shot, a department's work on a group of shots (“Roto – wide shots, 40 shots”), anything with days and a rate. Each line has its department, complexity, number of shots, days per shot and day rate. Picking a complexity fills in the studio's days per shot for it, which you can still change on the line. Add shots from tracker… adds one line per shot the project already has on the dashboard (omitted and cancelled shots are left out).

The editor totals as you type: artist days, cost, the margin and what it earns, the price, any discount, tax and the total the client pays. Every figure is exact to the paisa or cent. Create bid stays switched off, saying why, until the bid makes sense — a line without a description, days or a day rate, or a margin above the studio's limit.

Currency and tax

A bid is in the studio's currency (Indian rupees unless the studio changed it) or in the client's: US dollars, euros or pounds. Every amount of a bid is shown in its own currency, and totals in different currencies are never added together. Rupee bids start with GST at the studio's rate (18% unless changed); bids in another currency start with no tax. Both can be changed on the bid. Bids made before currencies were recorded are in US dollars.

Sending, winning and losing

StatusMeans
DraftBeing worked on. Only a draft can be changed.
SentWith the client. Mark sent records when.
Won / LostThe client's answer, with who recorded it and when.
SupersededA newer revision exists. Kept, read-only.

Marking a bid Won or Lost — or reopening one that was decided — needs the Approve bids ability, and asks first. Nobody decides a bid they made themselves, except Admin and Developer. Reopen as draft (under More) puts a bid back to draft.

Revisions

A bid that was sent or decided opens read-only. To change it, make a New revision: a draft copy (v2, v3…) you can edit, while the earlier revision is kept exactly as it was. The list shows the latest revision of each bid; tick All revisions to see the others. Compare revisions… lists the lines added, removed and changed between two revisions, and how the price moved. Duplicate to project… starts a new draft for another project from the same lines.

The cards

Open pipeline is draft and sent work: only the newest open bid per project counts, because several drafts for one job are versions of one price, not several jobs. Won is every won bid. Archived and superseded bids count in neither.

Tracking a won bid

Select a won bid and Tracking below the list compares it with the project's dashboard, department by department: the days bid, the days planned on the dashboard's tasks, the days delivered (tasks in a done status), the actual days where they were recorded, how much of the bid is burned and what remains — in days and in money at the bid's own rates. A department planned or spent above its bid is red. It also lists shots that were bid but are not on the dashboard, and dashboard shots the bid never priced. Export… saves the table.

Create shots on the dashboard… (under More, for a won bid) adds the shots the bid names — lines with a Shot — to the project's dashboard, with each department's bid days. Shots already there are left exactly as they are.

Archive, export and settings

Archive… takes bids out of the list and the pipeline but keeps them, with their history; tick Archived to see them and Restore them. Archiving offers Undo. Only an Admin or Developer can delete a draft for good, and only one that was never sent, decided or revised — the gap between what was bid and what the dashboard recorded is the best input to the next bid. Export list… saves the bids shown as CSV or Excel; Export bid as PDF… prints one bid for the client (cost and margin are left out).

Bidding settings… (for people who approve bids) holds the studio's figures for every workstation: the day rate per currency, days per shot by complexity, the default and highest margin, and the GST rate. Bids already made keep their own figures.

attendance.title: Attendance
attendance.content:
Attendance

Punch in when you start and out when you finish. The buttons only offer the next step that makes sense: Punch in, then Punch out (it asks first), then Punch in again if you come back the same day — that starts a second session, and the day's hours add both together.

Closing Slate or signing out never punches you out. Signing in starts your day if it has not started yet; it never starts a second session by itself.

Working from home

Tick Working from home today before or after punching in; the day's record follows the box.

Your month

Pick any month under My month. Each day says what it was: present, late (only on a day you were expected in), short day, on leave (approved leave shows here), holiday or weekly off, absent, worked a day off, or a missing punch. The legend uses exactly the colours the tables use.

If you forgot to punch out

The next time you punch in, a forgotten day is closed at the studio's automatic punch-out time — unless that would be before your punch-in, in which case the day is marked missing punch-out for HR instead of being given hours you did not work. You cannot edit your own record; ask HR.

Supervisors

If you approve leave, My team shows the month of the people who report to you, read-only.

HR

  • Team overview: everybody, sorted by name, with search and department / manager / location filters. Each person is judged against their own location's holidays.
  • Double-click a day to correct it. Times are picked, an out time before the in time needs Ends next day, and a reason is required; the day keeps who changed it, why and what it said before (shown on hover). Clear day removes a record and notes it in the audit log.
  • Export writes the month as shown: day codes (P, L, S, A, LV, H, WO, M, W) with hours, totals, overnight shifts counted properly, and a note when today's open sessions are included.
  • Import biometric reads the machine's export; a night shift becomes one day, and every line or day that could not be used is listed with the reason.

Comp-off

Where the studio operates comp-off, it is earned from this record: a weekly off or public holiday worked (by your own location's calendar), or a long enough day. Days closed by the automatic punch-out never earn it.

leave.title: Leave
leave.content:
Leave

Two screens sit behind this entry: My leave for everybody, and the Queue for people who decide on other people's leave.

My leave

FigureMeans
Paid leave availableWhat you can still take. Casual, Sick and Earned share one balance. Everything you have asked for or booked is already taken off; an overdrawn balance shows as overdrawn.
EarnedTwo days for every completed month since you joined (or what was carried plus this year, after a year end)
Awaiting approvalDays held by requests nobody has decided yet
BookedApproved leave still to come
Comp offOnly where the studio operates it

Request leave shows the cost before you send it, including the sandwich rule: a working day between two non-working days costs the whole block, judged on the working days you take — asking for more days never costs less. A half day is the first or the second half of one day. Past dates are allowed and marked as retrospective.

After sending, Slate says whose queue it went to. Waiting on names that person; Decision shows what the approvers wrote.

Withdraw cancels a request still waiting. For approved leave that has not started it asks HR to cancel it; the days come back once HR agree.

The queue

It opens on what is waiting on you. Selecting a request shows its working and sandwich days, the person's balance before and after, both notes, and who else from the team is away then. Nobody can approve their own request.

A request whose supervisor cannot act (nobody recorded, or somebody who cannot approve leave) goes straight to HR. HR can also decide a request still waiting on a supervisor, for them, and that is recorded. If somebody withdrew a request while you were looking at it, Approve says so instead of bringing it back.

HR tools

  • Holidays: the calendar leave is charged against. After adding or removing a holiday Slate offers to re-cost requests still waiting.
  • Year end: finished years only, closed in order, previewed first. People with no joining date are listed, not closed, unless you include them. Years nobody closed still have the carry-forward cap applied to balances.
  • Comp off earned: what attendance says people have earned back.
  • Grant project rest: project rest is granted by HR, not requested.
  • Revoke: take back approved leave, with a reason the person sees.

joining_leaving.title: Joining & Leaving
joining_leaving.content:
Joining & Leaving

One checklist, read in two directions. HR and IT each see their own half. Somebody joining and leaving has two rows, one per list, with the joining date or last working day beside their name.

Starting somebody

HR only. Start joining / Start leaving: pick the person (they need an account on Users & Roles), employment and department from the same lists Users & Roles uses, and the date. If a joining date is already on record Slate shows it and asks before changing it — leave accrues from it. A list started by mistake can be cancelled; ticked lines stay as the record.

Ticking lines

Each line shows who ticked it and when.

Machines

IT only. Issue machine lists free machines with type, GPU, CPU, RAM and location. Issuing to somebody whose last day has passed, or who is on the leaving list, asks first. When somebody leaves, every machine they hold gets its own Return line, and Workstation returned is only ticked once nothing is out.

Kit not returned

A red card appears when a machine is still out with somebody whose last day has passed.

it_support.title: IT Support
it_support.content:
IT Support

Report a problem to IT and follow what happens to it. If you work in IT you also get the Queue: every ticket in the studio, worst first.

Raising one

Report a problem. Pick what kind of problem it is, give it a one-line summary, and say what you were doing and what happened. If a machine is issued to you in Hardware, its name is added to the ticket for you.

Two questions decide how fast it gets picked up. Answer them honestly rather than strategically — you do not choose the priority, and that is exactly what keeps the queue worth trusting.

Cannot workWorkaroundCan wait
Whole studioP1P2P2
A departmentP2P3P3
One personP3P3P4

When you send it you get the ticket number and what IT aim for. The list shows your open tickets; tick Include closed for the old ones.

Afterwards

Select a ticket and press Open (or Enter, or double-click) to read the conversation and reply; Ctrl+Enter sends. New replies appear while it is open, and the bell tells you when IT pick it up, reply, need your answer or resolve it.

When IT need something from you the ticket says Waiting on you, sits at the top of your list with a banner, and the IT Support entry in the sidebar shows a count. Their clock is paused until you answer; your reply puts the ticket straight back with them.

On a resolved ticket: This is fixed closes it, Still broken - reopen puts it back in the queue (a reply does the same). Withdraw closes a ticket you no longer need help with.

The promise (SLA)

PriorityRespond withinFix within
P1 Critical15 minutes4 hours, day or night
P2 High30 working minutes8 working hours
P3 Medium2 working hours3 working days
P4 Low4 working hours5 working days

Working time is the studio's working hours — Monday to Saturday, 10:00 to 19:00 unless the studio has changed them in Settings (Studio Currency, Rates & Hours). Sundays and studio holidays do not count. A P1 is measured around the clock. Time a ticket spends waiting on the person who raised it is not counted against IT.

Response is attention; resolution is a fix. Picking a ticket up or replying to it is the response.

Working the queue (IT)

Sorted the way you should work it: breached first, then at risk (the last quarter of a response window, the last fifth of a fix window), then by priority and time left. Click a heading to sort by it; Worst first puts the order back. Paused tickets (waiting on the requester) come after the live ones and never count as breached.

The figures — Unresolved, Breached, At risk, Unassigned, Mine — are filters: click one to see those tickets. Filter by status, owner, priority and category; search by words, a person's name or #number.

ActionDoes
New ticketLogs a ticket for somebody else (a phone call, a walk-up). It is theirs; you are noted as having logged it
Assign to mePicks the ticket up and stops the response clock. Asks first if a colleague has it
Set status…Opens on the current status. Resolved and Closed need a note for the requester, which goes into the conversation
More > Assign to… / UnassignHand a ticket to a colleague, or put it back in the pool
More > Change priority…With a reason, kept in the conversation
More > Responded by phoneFor an answer given by phone or in person; a written reply counts by itself
SLA reportPer month and priority: tickets resolved, how many kept each promise, median time to fix

In the conversation, tick Internal note to keep a note among IT; the person who raised the ticket never sees it. Your reply to an unassigned ticket picks it up for you. Every status change, assignment and priority change is written into the conversation, so both sides can see what happened.

Attachments are not available yet: paste the text of an error, or put a screenshot on the studio share and say where.

hardware.title: Hardware
hardware.content:
Hardware

Machines the studio owns, who has them, and their state.

Status

StatusMeans
AvailableIn service and free to issue
ActiveIn service and issued to somebody (the loan record says who)
RepairWith a workshop. Cannot be issued; collecting it back keeps the flag
Retired, Lost, DisposedEnd of life. Hidden unless you tick Show retired; never offered for issue

Active and Available are never typed: in Edit you choose In service and Slate works out which from the loan record. Choosing Repair or an end-of-life state for a machine somebody has asks to collect it back first.

The figures at the top — Machines, Available, In repair, Out on loan — filter the list when you click them.

Finding a machine

Search by machine name, person, location, CPU or GPU, filter by status, and click a column heading to sort (RAM and storage sort by size). The list refreshes when somebody else changes it and keeps your selection. The Warranty column turns amber within 60 days of the end and red once it has passed.

Issue and Collect

Select a machine and press Issue to… to hand it to somebody (type part of their name), or Collect to take it back. Both write the loan record that the leaving checklist reads, so when that person leaves, Slate already knows which machine to ask for. History lists everyone who has had the machine and when.

Adding and changing machines

Add machine: the name it has on the network (letters, digits, - _ .), type, serial number, asset tag, CPU, GPU, RAM and storage in GB, location, purchase and warranty dates. A new machine is Available, or in Repair.

Double-click a machine (or Edit) to change it. Rename… in Edit renames it and moves its loan history, checklist lines and deployment records with it.

Sync from Live Ops adds machines running Slate that the inventory does not know yet, unassigned, and refreshes the specification of known ones. It never replaces something you typed with an empty value, and it names any report it could not read.

Delete is for a machine added by mistake. A machine that has ever been issued keeps its history: set it to Retired, Lost or Disposed instead.

What to check now and then

Machines out with somebody who has left: Joining & Leaving shows these as Kit not returned.

licences.title: Licences
licences.content:
Licences

Not an inventory. This screen answers the two questions you actually get asked, and they cost money in opposite directions:

  • Are we licensed? More people working than seats bought is what ends in an audit letter.
  • Are we paying for seats nobody uses? Invisible until somebody looks at the peak rather than the total.

Peak, not total

The honest measure of a floating licence is peak concurrent use, and the only way to know it is to have written the number down repeatedly.

Record usage: pick the licence (two contracts of one product are told apart by seats, renewal date and contract number), the seats in use, and when the licence server said it — now, or earlier (last Friday's peak). Take readings when the studio is busy; a quiet-afternoon number makes an over-subscribed licence look healthy.

Import from licence server… reads a report saved from the licence server — FlexLM lmstat -a or RLM rlmstat -a — and turns it into readings. Each product is matched to a licence, which you can change or skip. Slate reads the text only; it does not contact the licence server.

Readings… shows every reading behind a licence's peak, as a chart against the seats bought. Select a wrong one to Correct or Delete it — one typo should not keep a licence over-subscribed for a year.

The window selector — 30 days, 90 days, a year — decides how far back the peak is measured, and is remembered.

The findings

FindingMeans
Over-subscribedPeak exceeded what we own (also with 0 seats bought). Outranks everything else
ExpiredAlready gone. Anyone relying on it is stuck right now
Renews soonInside the studio's renewal window (45 days unless changed). Decide before purchasing needs lead time
Under-usedPeak never reaches 60% of what was bought. A smaller renewal is suggested, with headroom
No readingsBought, never measured. Nothing to renew against except the invoice

Every row also says what it means in a sentence, with the cost of the unused seats when the licence has an annual cost.

The figures at the top

Over-subscribed and Renewing or expired are the two to act on (a licence that is both counts in both). Seats bought counts licences that have not expired. Spare seats are paid for above peak use, with what they cost a year.

A licence's details

Add licence / Edit: software, contract or PO number (needed when another licence has the same name), seats bought, renewal date or No expiry, annual cost and currency (rupees unless the contract is in dollars, euros or pounds), vendor and notes. Remove says how many readings go with it.

IT are reminded through the bell when a licence enters the renewal window, 14 days before it renews and when it expires — once each.

People who approve renewals see this screen read-only; changing it is for IT.

deployment.title: Deployment
deployment.content:
Deployment

A record of what was installed where — Nuke 16 on WS-12, a plugin update on the comp floor. Slate does not install software itself; this is the log IT keep so the studio knows what each machine should have.

Recording one

  1. Record deployment: the package, its version, notes, and the machines — several at once, separated by commas, completed from Hardware. A name Hardware does not know is questioned. One record is written per machine, as Pending.
  2. When you know how it went, select it and press Mark success or Mark failed (which asks why, for the notes). Who marked it and when is kept; changing an outcome already recorded asks first.

Double-click a record (or Edit) to correct it; Delete removes one recorded by mistake.

The figures count every record (Installs recorded), the success rate of the ones with an outcome, and those Awaiting outcome — click it to see them.

Finding one

Search by package, version, machine, person or notes, filter by status, and sort by any column. Other people's records appear without a restart.

Updating Slate itself

New versions of Slate reach machines through the studio's update path, not through this screen. Check Workspace Info on a machine for the version it is actually running.

users_roles.title: Users & Roles
users_roles.content:
Users & Roles

Who exists, and what each of them can reach. HR see Users; the people who edit permissions see Roles & Permissions.

Roles decide screens

A role carries the tabs it opens and the things it may do. A tab somebody has no business on is absent, not greyed out. A change to somebody's roles shows the next time they sign in.

Who may give what

Admin and Developer may give anything. Anybody else can only hand on what they hold themselves: they cannot tick Full access or the sensitive abilities (managing users and permissions, system administration, studio settings, destructive test tools, deleting projects), cannot change a role they hold, and cannot give somebody a role more powerful than their own — or change the account of somebody more powerful. Boxes you cannot give are switched off, and the reason is in the tooltip.

Adding somebody

Add user creates a new account and nothing else: a username already in use is refused. Usernames are 2 to 40 letters, numbers, dots, dashes or underscores. Reports to offers only people who approve or keep leave; somebody with no valid approver has their leave go to HR, and the list marks them. Editing can empty a field as well as change it. Then start them in Joining & Leaving.

Importing many

Import reads Username and Display Name, and also Department, Joined, Reports To, Location, Employment and Role when the file has them (the template does). Each value is checked and the preview says what will be set. There is no default role; admin-level roles are never offered. Ticking Update existing people previews and applies profile changes only — never passwords or roles — so an exported list can be edited and imported back.

Roles

Ticks wait for Save changes; Revert puts them back. Roles can be renamed — the people who hold one keep it.

Passwords

Stored as one-way hashes. You can reset somebody's password; you cannot read it, and neither can anyone else, including an administrator.

Somebody who has left

Deactivate rather than delete. The account is switched off, their attendance, leave and other history are kept, and they disappear from lists and pickers. Show deactivated brings them back into view, and Reactivate switches the account on again. A person whose last working day has passed counts as deactivated too.

Deactivating is refused while the person still has leave waiting for a decision or a machine issued — handle those first. You cannot deactivate yourself. Delete is only for an account made by mistake that has no history at all.

admin_panel.title: Admin Panel
admin_panel.content:
Admin Panel

The studio's machinery: the workstations, their logs and the database. Admins and developers see all three pages. A supervisor sees Live Ops only, read-only.

Live Ops

Every workstation running Slate reports in about every 30 seconds: who is signed in, how full its disks are and its specification. A machine that misses its reports turns Not responding (amber) and, after five minutes, Offline (red) with when it was last seen - it stays on the page. The strip at the top counts each state (click one to show only those); search, the status filter and sorting narrow the grid. Double-click a machine, or use its … button, for its system specs.

Fleet report saves every machine's latest report as Excel, CSV or JSON. Admins can also send a message to every workstation, start the API gateway, restart or shut down a machine (it asks, names the machine and is written to the audit trail) and clear every workstation's caches (Wipe caches).

Audit Logs

Workstation logs - the log each machine sends in, with its level, source and message; filter to warnings or errors, search, and pick a line to read all of it. Change history - who changed which field of which shot or record, and when, with a date range, paging and export. Audit trail - sign-ins, user and role changes and admin actions.

Data Center

The studio database itself: an overview, its tables and the SQL box. Edits are saved row by row (tables without a primary key are read-only) and written to the change history. Deleting a row names it first; purging the stock library is under Data maintenance and needs PURGE typed. Changes here bypass every screen's checks and affect everybody at once.

tester.title: Tester Panel
tester.content:
Tester Panel

Tools for checking Slate itself. Nothing here is needed to do a day's work. Everything writes into the Test folder chosen above the tabs - a scratch folder, never a project or a studio share. Folders the panel creates hold a .slate_tester file, and the destructive tools act only on such folders. Deleting, setting file dates, runs over 1 GB, VACUUM and Simulate crash are for developers.

Data generator

Dummy files of the chosen types and size, with the total shown before you start; it checks the free disk space and asks above 5 GB. The button turns into Stop while it runs.

Workflow sim

A test incoming structure with an Excel sheet, in a new TEST folder (an existing one is never replaced), with optional extra levels, scans and image sequences.

Deep folders

Deep and wide folder trees, as deep as Windows' path limit allows.

Analysis

Check a folder against the database, compare two folders, or list files that are on disk but not in the database. Database health: an integrity check, and VACUUM to compact it.

Diagnostics

The live log while the tab is open, and 1,000 small files for load checks.

System

The permission matrix (role by tab, with abilities), a config sandbox that points this session at another server root or cache until you reset it, and Set file dates.

Automation

A regression run: 50 images are created, ingested into the stock library and counted; it says passed or failed with the numbers, then removes its test rows.

Utilities

Delete the test folder - only one the panel created - after saying how many files it holds.

settings.title: Settings
settings.content:
Settings

Two kinds of setting live here. Your preferences apply to you on this machine. Studio settings apply to everybody and are shown only to the people allowed to change them (Admin, Developer and IT).

Your preferences

  • Remember last folders — reopen the folders you last used.
  • Start Build & Ingest in dry run — it shows what it would do and writes nothing.
  • Theme and UI scale — how Slate looks on this screen.
  • Open Nuke as — which Nuke opens when you open a shot in Nuke.

The bar at the top says when something is unsaved: Save changes, Discard, or Reset to defaults. Preferences apply at once; the theme, server root and database are used from the next start.

Studio settings

Studio Policy — what counts as late and how long a normal day is. Attendance and Leave both read these, for everybody.

Paths & Connections — the project and server roots, the studio logo in the header, and where the studio database is (host, port, name, user). The database details are stored in this machine's Slate configuration file, so an update keeps them. If Slate starts in LOCAL MODE, look here — though it is usually the server or the network rather than these values.

Runtime status and maintenance

Runtime Status shows which database this machine reached, whether the shared folder is reachable and whether offline changes are waiting to sync. System Maintenance checks for a newer Slate, makes a project report, backs up a project and opens the log folder for IT.

Your password

Change it from your name in the header. It is stored as a one-way hash: nobody, including an administrator, can read it back.
